Infection mainly results from trauma to the skin, and may spread locally through the lymphatic system to surrounding tissues, progressively destroying connective tissue and bone. Mycetomas caused by fungi such as Madurella mycetomatis, M. grisea, or Pseudallescheria boydii are called eumycetomas. Those caused by the filamentous bacteria, actinomycetes, are called actinomycetomas and are discussed on p.180. Eumycetomas do not heal spontaneously and are poorly responsive to treatment. They often require both surgical excision and antifungal therapy. Itraconazole or ketocona- zole are recommended as first-line antifungals for eumyc- etomas and the duration of treatment depends on the sever- ity of the infection and ranges from a few months to years. Itraconazole has resulted in good clinical responses and low recurrence rates. Paracoccidioidomycosis Paracoccidioidomycosis (South American blastomycosis) is caused by an infection with the fungus Paracoccidioides brasiliensis. The disease occurs mainly in inhabitants of Central and South America. Infection is thought to be by inhalation and may remain dormant for long periods. While most primary infections are subclinical, some may be progressive and severe, particularly in immunocompro- mised patients. Paracoccidioidomycosis usually presents as a chronic infection affecting the lungs. Disseminated disease may affect the skin, mucous membranes, gastroin- testinal tract, reticuloendothelial system, and adrenals, and may be acute or chronic. Relatively mild cases may be treated with oral ketoconazole or itraconazole for 6 to 12 months or longer. Itraconazole allows shorter treatment courses and lower doses than ketoconazole; relapse rates are also lower.
